DIY or hired work: separate actual cash savings from the value of personal time

Compare all-in task costs, genuine earnings forgone and non-work hours. Keep a subjective value for personal time visible without turning it into an extra bill.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare actual cash consequences with a separate value for personal time

Interactive planning lab

Cash-resource saving from DIY$900
Additional personal hours used by DIY45.0
DIY saving after the separate subjective time valuation-$100

Original hypothetical comparison of completing the same task yourself or hiring it out. The quote and DIY outlays include all known taxes and fees. New tools are paid in full, with no resale or later-use credit. Only the entered share of DIY hours actually removes paid work, valued at independently entered after-tax earnings lost; the other DIY hours use non-work time. Hiring uses the entered coordination hours from non-work time only. The time-value input is a subjective valuation of non-work hours, not an extra invoice, payroll amount or claim that all free time could be sold for wages. Cash-resource totals include vendor outlays plus actual earnings forgone. Combined totals add the separate subjective time value once. No skill assessment, quality difference, project failure, safety guidance, financing, insurance, warranty value, tax deduction or other work opportunity is modeled.

The central idea

Only hours that actually remove paid work create the modeled earnings loss. Non-work time can still matter to the decision, but its subjective value belongs in a separate comparison from cash outlays.

01

Compare the same completed task before comparing prices

A decision to complete a task yourself can change both money and personal time. A lower materials bill alone does not describe the full cash effect, and assigning a wage to every free hour can misstate it in the other direction.

Begin with a comparable scope. The federal Office of Consumer Affairs renovation guide emphasizes detailed work and contract information. Here, the hired quote and the DIY alternative are assumed to deliver the same defined task. The model does not assess quality, qualifications or whether a particular job is appropriate for DIY.

Restore the example to use a CAD 3,000 all-in hired price, CAD 1,200 of DIY materials and CAD 300 of new tools and other upfront costs. All known taxes and fees are already included. The tools receive no resale or future-use credit in this example, so the entire initial outlay remains in the cash comparison.

02

Identify paid work that would actually be lost

The DIY task takes fifty personal hours. The selected 40% share means twenty of those hours genuinely displace paid work that would otherwise be available. At independently entered after-tax earnings of CAD 30 per displaced hour, the household forgoes CAD 600 of take-home income.

The other thirty hours come from non-work time. They may be valuable, but the model does not assume those hours could automatically have been sold at the person’s wage. A fixed-salary employee doing a task on a free weekend might enter a zero displaced-work share even if their usual hourly-equivalent salary is high.

The distinction depends on the actual alternative, not simply an employment contract’s headline pay. A reduction in overtime, a cancelled paid shift or foregone billable work can create a cash effect. Free time that would not have produced earnings does not create the same missing cash inflow. Tax and work-related costs should already be reflected in the independently entered net earnings amount.

03

Reconcile the cash saving without pricing leisure twice

The DIY cash-resource cost is CAD 1,200 of materials plus CAD 300 of new tools plus CAD 600 of earnings actually forgone, for CAD 2,100. Compared with the CAD 3,000 hired price, this produces a CAD 900 cash-resource saving.

The waterfall retains the distinction between cash spent and cash not earned. The CAD 600 is not another invoice from a supplier; it is a reduction in household inflow. Both effects matter to how much money remains available after the task.

No charge for the remaining thirty DIY hours appears in this cash bridge. Adding a subjective leisure value here and then adding it again in a broader comparison would count it twice. Likewise, a work hour already valued through lost after-tax earnings should not receive a second charge as a non-work hour.

04

Add a subjective time value as a separate layer

The example independently values each non-work hour at CAD 40. Thirty DIY non-work hours then have a subjective value of CAD 1,200. Hiring the task uses five non-work coordination hours, valued at CAD 200.

Adding those separate time values to cash-resource costs gives CAD 3,300 for DIY and CAD 3,200 for hiring. The broader comparison therefore favors hiring by CAD 100 under that preference, even though DIY saves CAD 900 in cash resources. The stacked bars show which part of each total is cash and which part is a non-cash valuation.

Those combined amounts are decision aids, not bank balances, invoices or investment returns. The CAD 40 input can reflect how strongly a person values time for rest, family or other activities. Another household can reasonably enter a different amount, including zero. The tool does not claim to discover an objective price for personal time.

05

Read the relevant time difference before dividing the cash saving

DIY uses forty-five more personal hours overall than the five-hour coordination alternative. However, twenty DIY hours have already been charged through the CAD 600 of lost earnings. The remaining non-work-time difference is thirty DIY hours minus five coordination hours, or twenty-five hours.

At the default cash saving, a subjective value of CAD 900 ÷ 25 = CAD 36 per additional non-work hour makes the broader totals equal. That threshold is a preference comparison after accounting for actual lost pay. It is not an hourly wage offer or a statement that the person can earn CAD 36 for every free hour.

The matrix instead stays cash-only. It changes task hours and the share that actually displaces paid work, holding the quote, materials, tools and after-tax earnings selected. Subjective time value does not affect those cells. This keeps an affordability question separate from how a household chooses to value its time.

06

Record what could change the comparison

Confirm comparable scope, materials, completion standard and included costs before using the result. A quote with cleanup or warranty provisions cannot be compared fairly with a DIY budget that silently omits the relevant work or cost. The model does not assign a warranty value or estimate the cost of redoing a failed task.

Check the time estimate against the household calendar. Hired-task coordination is assumed to use non-work time only; if it also displaces paid work, another earnings-loss entry is needed. New tool resale, later reuse, borrowing costs and differences in completion dates can also change the analysis. They should be added explicitly rather than treated as invisible benefits or expenses.

The four views support a transparent decision: the hours split, the cash bridge, the separate time valuation and the displaced-work sensitivity. A household can then see whether DIY is affordable, how much cash it would preserve, and what personal time it requires. The calculation does not decide how much that time should matter to the person making the choice.
